questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Artery supplying posterior 1/3 of spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The posterior spinal artery supplies the posterior third of the spinal cord, running along the dorsal surface to provide blood to the dorsal horns and posterior columns.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal artery supplies the posterior third of the spinal cord.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior spinal artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Origin of anterior spinal artery:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery is formed by the union of two vessels, each arising from the corresponding vertebral artery, creating a single midline artery that descends along the anterior median fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery originates from the vertebral arteries as a common trunk.
questions.modelAnswer: Single artery formed by union of two anterior spinal arteries, each from vertebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Origin of posterior spinal artery:
questions.explanation: The posterior spinal artery typically arises from either the vertebral artery directly or from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), forming paired vessels that supply the posterior spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal artery may originate from vertebral artery or PICA.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral artery or PICA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Origin of radicular arteries:
questions.explanation: Radicular arteries arise segmentally from various aortic branches including vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, and first lumbar arteries, following nerve roots to supply the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries have segmental origins from aortic branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, 1st lumbar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 6 veins draining spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord venous drainage follows a symmetrical pattern with anteromedian and posteromedian veins running vertically, plus four additional veins accompanying the ventral and dorsal nerve roots.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord has six longitudinal veins: anteromedian, posteromedian, and four radicular veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteromedian, posteromedian, four veins along ventral and dorsal roots.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete transverse section:
questions.explanation: A complete spinal cord transection produces different clinical pictures depending on level: above C5 causes respiratory death; between C5-T1 causes quadriplegia; below T1 causes paraplegia.
questions.keyConcept: Complete cord section effects vary by level: quadriplegia (C5-T1), paraplegia (below T1).
questions.modelAnswer: Above C5: death; Between C5-T1: quadriplegia; Below T1: paraplegia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Hemisection:
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection) causes ipsilateral motor loss and all sensory loss at the lesion level, ipsilateral proprioceptive loss below the lesion, and contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes ipsilateral motor and contralateral pain loss below lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: At lesion: ipsilateral loss of all sensations, ipsilateral LMNL; Below lesion ipsilateral: loss of proprioception, UMNL; Below lesion contralateral: loss of pain and temperature.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior spinal artery occlusion:
questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery occlusion produces bilateral upper motor neuron signs below the lesion and bilateral loss of pain/temperature with preserved proprioception due to intact posterior columns.
questions.keyConcept: ASA occlusion: bilateral motor loss, pain loss, preserved proprioception.
questions.modelAnswer: Bilateral UMNL below lesion, bilateral loss of pain and temperature, preservation of proprioception and touch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Parts of neostriatum:
questions.explanation: The neostriatum (striatum proper) consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen, separated by the internal capsule but functionally interconnected as part of the basal ganglia motor loop.
questions.keyConcept: Neostriatum = caudate nucleus + putamen.
questions.modelAnswer: Caudate and Putamen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Parts of paleostriatum:
questions.explanation: The paleostriatum refers to the globus pallidus, which is divided into internal (GPi) and external (GPe) segments that serve as the main output nuclei of the basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Paleostriatum = globus pallidus internus and externus.
questions.modelAnswer: Globus pallidus internal and external.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Blood supply of basal ganglia:
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia receive blood supply from central branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, which penetrate the brain substance to supply the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia supplied by branches of anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Central branches of anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Venous drainage of basal ganglia:
questions.explanation: The thalamostriate vein drains the basal ganglia and thalamus, carrying blood to the internal cerebral vein and ultimately the vein of Galen.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamostriate vein provides venous drainage for basal ganglia.
questions.modelAnswer: Thalamostriate vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete: Head
questions.explanation: The caudate nucleus has three parts: the head bulges into the lateral ventricle's anterior horn, the body forms part of the floor, and the tail runs along the roof of the inferior horn.
questions.keyConcept: Caudate nucleus anatomy: head in anterior horn, body in floor, tail in inferior horn roof.
questions.modelAnswer: of caudate bulges into anterior horn of lateral ventricle; body lies in floor of body of lateral ventricle; tail lies in roof of inferior horn of lateral ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 lobes (functional):
questions.explanation: The cerebellum's functional lobes include archicerebellum (vestibular coordination), paleocerebellum (postural control), and neocerebellum (skilled movements).
questions.keyConcept: Three functional cerebellar lobes: archi-, paleo-, and neocerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: Archicerebellum, paleocerebellum, neocerebellum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Archicerebellum formed of:
questions.explanation: The archicerebellum, the oldest functional region, is formed by the flocculi and nodule, which together constitute the vestibular cerebellum controlling balance and eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: Archicerebellum = flocculus and nodule of inferior vermis.
questions.modelAnswer: 2 flocculi and nodule (part of inferior vermis).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Paleocerebellum formed of:
questions.explanation: The paleocerebellum, controlling posture and gait, is formed by the vermal portion and paravermal zones of the cerebellar hemispheres, receiving proprioceptive input from the body.
questions.keyConcept: Paleocerebellum = vermis and paravermal zones for postural control.
questions.modelAnswer: Vermal part and 2 paravermal parts of cerebellar hemisphere.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Neocerebellum formed of:
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum, the largest and most recent functional region, is formed by the lateral parts of the cerebellar hemispheres and is responsible for planning and executing voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum = lateral cerebellar hemisphere for skilled movements.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral parts of cerebellar hemisphere.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 4 cerebellar nuclei:
questions.explanation: The four deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial are: dentate (largest), emboliform, globose, and fastigial, each projecting to different thalamic and brainstem targets.
questions.keyConcept: Four cerebellar nuclei: dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial.
questions.modelAnswer: Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arteries supplying cerebellum:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum receives blood from three paired arteries: superior cerebellar (SCA), anterior inferior cerebellar (AICA), and posterior inferior cerebellar (PICA) arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellum supplied by SCA, AICA, and PICA.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior cerebellar, anterior inferior cerebellar, posterior inferior cerebellar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Veins draining cerebellum:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar venous drainage is divided into superior cerebellar veins (draining to straight sinus) and inferior cerebellar veins (draining to transverse and sigmoid sinuses).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar veins drain to straight, transverse, and sigmoid sinuses.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior cerebellar veins and inferior cerebellar veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 4 afferent fibers of ICP:
questions.explanation: The four afferent fibers of the inferior cerebellar peduncle are: posterior spinocerebellar, dorsal external arcuate, ventral external arcuate, and olivocerebellar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: ICP afferents: posterior spinocerebellar, both arcuate, olivocerebellar.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior spinocerebellar, dorsal external arcuate, ventral external arcuate, olivocerebellar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Efferent fibers of ICP:
questions.explanation: Efferent fibers of the inferior cerebellar peduncle include cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebelloreticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebello-olivary fibers (to inferior olive).
questions.keyConcept: ICP efferents: cerebellovestibular, cerebelloreticular, cerebello-olivary.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellovestibular, cerebelloreticular, cerebello‑olivary.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Afferent fiber of MCP:
questions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries corticopontocerebellar fibers, the largest afferent pathway to the cerebellum, originating from the pontine nuclei receiving cerebral cortex input.
questions.keyConcept: MCP afferent is corticopontocerebellar pathway from pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Corticopontocerebellar fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Afferent fibers of SCP:
questions.explanation: Afferent fibers of the superior cerebellar peduncle include anterior spinocerebellar fibers (carrying proprioceptive data from lower body) and tectocerebellar fibers (from superior colliculus).
questions.keyConcept: SCP afferents: anterior spinocerebellar and tectocerebellar fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinocerebellar, tectocerebellar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Efferent fibers of SCP:
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle carries four efferent pathways: fastigioreticular, cerebellorubral, dentatothalamic, and dentatorubrothalamic fibers projecting to thalamus and brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: SCP efferents: fastigioreticular, cerebellorubral, dentatothalamic, dentatorubrothalamic.
questions.modelAnswer: Fastigioreticular, cerebellorubral, dentatothalamic, dentatorubrothalamic.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 external features of ventral medulla:
questions.explanation: The ventral medulla's three external features are the pyramid (motor decussation), olive (olivary nucleus), and inferior cerebellar peduncle containing ascending sensory fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral medulla features: pyramid, olive, inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer: Pyramid, Olive, ICP.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cranial nerves on ventral medulla:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves associated with the ventral medulla are CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), CN XI (accessory), and CN XII (hypoglossal), emerging in order from above downward.
questions.keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: 9, 10, 11, 12.
questions.modelAnswer: Glossopharyngeal (9), Vagus (10), Accessory (11), Hypoglossal (12).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 external features of ventral pons:
questions.explanation: The ventral pons displays three characteristic features: the middle cerebellar peduncle laterally, the basilar artery groove centrally, and transverse grooves indicating underlying fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral pons features: middle cerebellar peduncle, basilar groove, transverse fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: MCP, Basilar artery sulcus, transverse grooves.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cranial nerves on ventral pons:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves associated with the ventral pons include CN V (trigeminal), CN VI (abducent), CN VII (facial), and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear), emerging at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine cranial nerves: 5, 6, 7, 8.
questions.modelAnswer: Trigeminal (5), Abducent (6), Facial (7), Vestibulocochlear (8).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerves affected by cerebellopontine angle tumor:
questions.explanation: A cerebellopontine angle tumor (typically acoustic neuroma) first affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) causing hearing loss and vertigo, then CN VII (facial) causing facial weakness.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumor affects cranial nerves 7 and 8.
questions.modelAnswer: Facial and Vestibulocochlear.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 4 structures winding around cerebral peduncle:
questions.explanation: Four structures wind around the cerebral peduncle: optic tract (medial), trochlear nerve (lateral), posterior cerebral artery (superior), and basal vein (dorsal).
questions.keyConcept: Structures around cerebral peduncle: optic tract, trochlear nerve, PCA, basal vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Optic tract, Trochlear nerve, Posterior cerebral artery, Basal vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is bounded anteriorly by the optic chiasma, anterolaterally by the optic tract, posterolaterally by the cerebral peduncle, and posteriorly by the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa boundaries: optic chiasma, optic tract, cerebral peduncle, upper pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: optic chiasma; Anterolateral: optic tract; Posterolateral: cerebral peduncle; Posterior: upper border of pons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Contents of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa contains the tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance (allowing blood vessels to penetrate), and the oculomotor nerve emerging between the cerebral peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Fossa contents: tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, perforated substance, oculomotor nerve.
questions.modelAnswer: Tuber cinereum, mamillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, oculomotor nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 elevations of closed medulla:
questions.explanation: The closed medulla (above the obex) displays three posterior elevations: the gracile tubercle (medial), cuneate tubercle (lateral), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the most lateral position.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla elevations: gracile, cuneate, inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer: Gracile, Cuneate, ICP.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Borders of open medulla:
questions.explanation: The open medulla's borders are defined by the medullary striae marking the base (floor of fourth ventricle), the apex continuous with the central canal, and the hypoglossal, vagal, and vestibular trigones forming the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Open medulla borders: striae at base, central canal at apex, trigones as floor.
questions.modelAnswer: Base: medullary striae; Apex: continuous with central canal; Floor: hypoglossal, vagal, and vestibular trigones.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Borders of back of pons:
questions.explanation: The posterior surface of the pons is bounded by the medullary striae at its base (marking the pontomedullary junction), the cerebral aqueduct superiorly at the apex, and the floor consisting of the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior pons bounded by: medullary striae (base), cerebral aqueduct (apex), medial eminence/facial colliculus/vestibular area (floor).
questions.modelAnswer: Base: medullary striae; Apex: cerebral aqueduct; Floor: medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: External features of back of midbrain:
questions.explanation: The posterior midbrain displays four colliculi: two superior colliculi (involved in visual reflexes) and two inferior colliculi (involved in auditory reflexes), collectively forming the tectal plate or quadrigeminal plate.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior midbrain: two superior and two inferior colliculi.
questions.modelAnswer: 2 superior and 2 inferior colliculi.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Roof of fourth ventricle:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle roof consists of two vela: the superior medullary velum (connecting the superior cerebellar peduncles) forms the upper roof, while the inferior medullary velum (with choroid plexus) forms the lower roof.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof: superior and inferior medullary vela.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: SCP and superior medullary velum; Inferiorly: inferior medullary velum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Floor of fourth ventricle:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle floor has two parts: the pontine part contains the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; the medullary part contains the hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of fourth ventricle: pontine (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area) and medullary (three trigones).
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine part (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area); Medullary part (hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, vestibular trigone).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lateral boundaries:
questions.explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle consist of the superior cerebellar peduncle superiorly, the inferior cerebellar peduncle and gracile/cuneate tracts inferiorly, and the lateral recess extending toward the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral boundaries: SCP above, ICP and dorsal columns below, lateral recess.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: SCP; Inferiorly: ICP + gracile and cuneate tracts; Lateral recess.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choroid plexus lies in:
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle lies in the lower part of the roof, formed by the inferior medullary velum and tela choroidea where blood vessels invaginate the pia mater.
questions.keyConcept: Choroid plexus of fourth ventricle lies in lower roof.
questions.modelAnswer: Lower part of roof of fourth ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: GSE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: General somatic efferent (GSE) cranial nerve nuclei include the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), abducent (CN VI), and hypoglossal (CN XII) nuclei supplying extraocular and tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: GSE column nuclei: CN 3, 4, 6, 12.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: SVE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: Special visceral efferent (SVE) nuclei include the motor nucleus of trigeminal (CN V), motor nucleus of facial (CN VII), and nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X, XI) supplying branchial arch-derived muscles.
questions.keyConcept: SVE column nuclei: motor nuclei of CN 5, 7, and nucleus ambiguus (9,10,11).
questions.modelAnswer: Motor nucleus of 5, Motor nucleus of 7, Nucleus ambiguus (9,10,11).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: GVE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: General visceral efferent (GVE) nuclei include the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III for pupil constriction), superior salivatory (CN VII), inferior salivatory (CN IX), and dorsal vagal nuclei (CN X).
questions.keyConcept: GVE column nuclei: Edinger-Westphal, superior/inferior salivatory, dorsal vagal.
questions.modelAnswer: Edinger‑Westphal (3), Superior salivatory (7), Inferior salivatory (9), Dorsal vagal (10).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Spinal part of accessory nerve supplies:
questions.explanation: The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, which are responsible for head movement and shoulder elevation.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
questions.modelAnswer: Sternomastoid and Trapezius.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Origin of spinal accessory:
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve originates from the spinal nucleus located in the ventral horn of the first five cervical segments (C1-C5), with fibers ascending through the foramen magnum to join the cranial root.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal accessory originates from ventral horn of upper 5 cervical segments.
questions.modelAnswer: Spinal nucleus in ventral horn of upper 5 cervical segments.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Muscles supplied by motor nucleus of trigeminal:
questions.explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve supplies the four muscles of mastication plus tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and the anterior belly of digastric.
questions.keyConcept: Motor V supplies mastication muscles, tensor tympani/palate, mylohyoid, anterior digastric.
questions.modelAnswer: 4 muscles of mastication, Tensor palate, Tensor tympani, Anterior belly of digastric, Mylohyoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arteries supplying medulla:
questions.explanation: The medulla receives blood from the anterior spinal artery, PICA (the largest branch), and direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, with additional contribution from posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Medulla supplied by anterior spinal, PICA, vertebral branches, and posterior spinal arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal, PICA, medullary branches of vertebral, posterior spinal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arteries supplying pons:
questions.explanation: The pons is primarily supplied by paramedian and circumferential branches of the basilar artery, which penetrate the ventral surface to supply pontine nuclei and fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Pons supplied by branches of basilar artery.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of basilar artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pontine hemorrhage causes:
questions.explanation: Pontine hemorrhage typically damages bilateral corticospinal and autonomic pathways, causing pinpoint pupils (loss of pupillary light reflex), hyperpyrexia (autonomic dysregulation), and quadriplegia.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine hemorrhage: pinpoint pupils, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia.
questions.modelAnswer: Pinpoint pupil, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arteries supplying midbrain:
questions.explanation: The midbrain receives blood from branches of the posterior cerebral artery (supplying the anterior and lateral regions) and branches of the superior cerebellar artery (supplying the posterior region).
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain supplied by posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery) causes contralateral spastic hemiplegia below the lesion, contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, and ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiplegia, proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue palsy.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia (flaccid), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, ipsilateral LMNL of tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lateral medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome from PICA occlusion) causes ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, hoarseness, and Horner syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral face, contralateral body sensory loss, ataxia, Horner syndrome.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral loss of pain/temp from face, contralateral loss from body, ipsilateral paralysis of palate/pharynx/larynx, loss of taste, ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fracture of anterior cranial fossa:
questions.explanation: Anterior cranial fossa fractures typically tear the cribriform plate, causing CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia; blood tracks into orbital contents producing subconjunctival hemorrhage and orbital ecchymosis.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior fossa fracture: CSF rhinorrhea, subconjunctival and orbital hemorrhage.
questions.modelAnswer: Bleeding and CSF rhinorrhea, orbital hemorrhage and subconjunctival hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fracture of middle cranial fossa:
questions.explanation: Middle cranial fossa fractures frequently involve the petrous temporal bone, causing CSF otorrhea, Battle sign (mastoid bruising), and commonly affecting CN VII and VIII with facial paralysis and hearing loss.
questions.keyConcept: Middle fossa fracture: CSF otorrhea, Battle sign, CN 7 and 8 involvement.
questions.modelAnswer: Bleeding and CSF otorrhea, CN 7 & 8 involvement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fracture of posterior cranial fossa:
questions.explanation: Posterior cranial fossa fractures allow blood to escape into the nape of neck and posterior triangle due to gravity, presenting with mastoid and neck bruising that tracks inferiorly.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior fossa fracture: blood tracks to nape and posterior triangle of neck.
questions.modelAnswer: Blood escapes into nape and posterior triangle of neck.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Attachments of falx cerebri:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri attaches superiorly to the crista galli and frontal crest, posteriorly to the tentorium's upper surface, along its upper border to the sagittal sulcus lips, and its free lower border encloses the inferior sagittal sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri attachments: crista galli, tentorium, sagittal sulcus, inferior sagittal sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex: crista galli and frontal crest; Base: upper surface of tentorium; Upper border: lips of sagittal sulcus; Lower free border: encloses inferior sagittal sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Attachments of falx cerebelli:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebelli attaches along its base to the tentorium cerebelli, at its apex to the foramen magnum margins, along its posterior border to the internal occipital crest, and is free anteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebelli: tentorium base, foramen magnum apex, occipital crest posteriorly, free anteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: Base: tentorium; Apex: margins of foramen magnum; Posterior border: internal occipital crest; Anterior border: free.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve supply of dura:
questions.explanation: The dura mater receives sensory innervation differently in each fossa: anterior fossa from anterior ethmoidal and maxillary nerves, middle fossa from maxillary and mandibular divisions, posterior fossa from meningeal branches of CN X, XII and C1-3.
questions.keyConcept: Dura innervation: anterior (V1,V2), middle (V2,V3), posterior (CN 10,12, C1-3).
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior fossa: anterior ethmoidal + maxillary; Middle fossa: maxillary + mandibular; Posterior fossa: meningeal branches of 10,12 and recurrent branches of C1-3.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Venous drainage of dura:
questions.explanation: Dural venous drainage occurs via meningeal veins (accompanying meningeal arteries) and diploic veins (within skull bones), which connect to both intracranial venous sinuses and external scalp veins.
questions.keyConcept: Dura drains via meningeal veins and diploic veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal veins and diploic veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Extradural vs Subdural hemorrhage:
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage results from middle meningeal artery rupture causing arterial bleeding with rapid accumulation and lucid interval, while subdural hemorrhage involves bridging veins causing slower venous accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Extradural: arterial (meningeal); Subdural: venous (bridging veins).
questions.modelAnswer: Extradural: arterial (middle meningeal); Subdural: venous.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Single sinuses:
questions.explanation: The single (unpaired) dural venous sinuses include the superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, and occipital sinuses, each lying in specific dural folds or along bone margins.
questions.keyConcept: Single sinuses: superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, occipital.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, occipital.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Paired sinuses:
questions.explanation: The paired dural sinuses include sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, and transverse sinuses, occurring on both sides of the cranial cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Paired sinuses: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior/inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.
questions.modelAnswer: Sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tributaries of superior sagittal sinus:
questions.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus receives tributaries from the superior cerebral veins, which drain the cerebral convexity, and communicates with arachnoid granulations that absorb CSF into venous blood.
questions.keyConcept: SSS tributaries: superior cerebral veins and arachnoid villi.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior cerebral veins, arachnoid villi.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: External relations of cavernous sinus:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus is related anteriorly to the superior orbital fissure, posteriorly to the petrous apex and crus cerebri, medially to the pituitary gland and sphenoid sinus, laterally to the temporal lobe, superiorly to the optic tract and ICA, and inferiorly to foramen lacerum.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus relations: orbital fissure anterior, petrous apex posterior, pituitary medially, temporal lobe laterally.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: superior orbital fissure; Posterior: apex of petrous temporal and crus cerebri; Medial: pituitary and sphenoid sinus; Lateral: temporal lobe; Superior: optic tract and ICA; Inferior: foramen lacerum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Structures inside cavernous sinus:
questions.explanation: Within the cavernous sinus run the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic division of trigeminal, maxillary division of trigeminal, and abducent nerves, along with the internal carotid artery.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus contents: CN 3,4,5V1,5V2,6, and internal carotid artery.
questions.modelAnswer: Oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic, maxillary, abducent nerves; ICA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tributaries of cavernous sinus:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus receives blood from the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins (connecting with facial venous drainage), the central retinal vein, and the superficial middle cerebral vein.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous tributaries: superior/inferior ophthalmic, central retinal, superficial middle cerebral veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior ophthalmic, inferior ophthalmic, central retinal, superficial middle cerebral.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Drainage of cavernous sinus:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus drains posteriorly via the superior petrosal sinus (to sigmoid sinus) and inferior petrosal sinus (to jugular bulb), providing outflow from the cranial venous system.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus drains via superior and inferior petrosal sinuses.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior and inferior petrosal sinuses.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Communications of cavernous sinus:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus communicates with the pterygoid plexus via emissary veins through the foramen ovale, with the facial vein via the superior ophthalmic vein, and with the opposite cavernous sinus via the intercavernous sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous communications: pterygoid plexus, facial vein, opposite cavernous sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: Pterygoid plexus via emissary vein; Facial vein via superior ophthalmic; Opposite side via intercavernous sinuses.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve piercing cribriform plate:
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve (CN I) consists of special sensory fibers that pierce the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to reach the olfactory bulb from the nasal mucosa, making it unique among cranial nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory nerve pierces cribriform plate to reach olfactory bulb.
questions.modelAnswer: Olfactory.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve through optic canal:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve (CN II) passes through the optic canal, carrying visual information from the retina to the lateral geniculate body, making it functionally part of the CNS rather than a true peripheral nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve (CN II) traverses the optic canal.
questions.modelAnswer: Optic nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve in front of crossing of tentorium margins:
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges in the interpeduncular fossa, anterior to the crossing of the tentorium margins, before dividing into superior and inferior branches that enter the orbit.
questions.keyConcept: Oculomotor nerve emerges anterior to tentorium crossing.
questions.modelAnswer: Oculomotor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve at crossing of tentorium margins:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve to exit posteriorly from the dorsal midbrain, crossing at the superior medullary velum at the tentorium margin level.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve exits posteriorly at tentorium crossing level.
questions.modelAnswer: Trochlear.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve through hypoglossal canal:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal, which lies above the foramen magnum, carrying motor fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve passes through hypoglossal canal above foramen magnum.
questions.modelAnswer: Hypoglossal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of cerebral part of ICA:
questions.explanation: The cerebral part of the internal carotid artery gives five branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, anterior cerebral, and middle cerebral arteries, supplying the orbit, diencephalon, and cerebral hemispheres.
questions.keyConcept: ICA cerebral branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, ACA, MCA.
questions.modelAnswer: Ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, anterior and middle cerebral.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of temporal fossa:
questions.explanation: The temporal fossa is bounded superiorly by the superior temporal line and inferiorly by the zygomatic arch, with the deep temporal fascia separating it from the temporalis muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Temporal fossa: superior temporal line above, zygomatic arch below.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: superior temporal line; Inferior: zygomatic arch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of infratemporal fossa:
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa is bounded laterally by the mandibular ramus, medially by the lateral pterygoid plate, anteriorly by the posterior maxilla, posteriorly by the styloid process, and superiorly by the greater wing of sphenoid.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa boundaries: mandible laterally, pterygoid plate medially, maxilla anteriorly, styloid posteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral: ramus of mandible; Medial: lateral pterygoid plate; Anterior: posterior maxilla; Posterior: styloid process; Superior: greater wing of sphenoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Communications of infratemporal fossa:
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa communicates superiorly with the middle cranial fossa via foramen ovale and spinosum, anteriorly with the orbit via inferior orbital fissure, medially with the pterygopalatine fossa via pterygomaxillary fissure, and with the temporal fossa deep to the zygomatic arch.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa communicates: middle cranial fossa, orbit, pterygopalatine fossa, temporal fossa.
questions.modelAnswer: With temporal fossa (deep to zygomatic arch); With middle cranial fossa (foramen ovale & spinosum); With orbit (inferior orbital fissure); With pterygopalatine fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve supply of muscles of mastication:
questions.explanation: All muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid) are innervated by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3), except the medial pterygoid which receives a branch from the trunk.
questions.keyConcept: Muscles of mastication: all by anterior division of V3 except medial pterygoid (trunk).
questions.modelAnswer: All by anterior division of mandibular nerve except medial pterygoid by trunk.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Actions of muscles of mastication:
questions.explanation: The muscles of mastication produce protrusion (lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid, masseter) except temporalis which retracts; elevation is produced by all except lateral pterygoid which depresses; medial and lateral pterygoid together produce side-to-side grinding movements.
questions.keyConcept: Mastication actions: protrusion (except temporalis), elevation (except lateral pterygoid), side-to-side movement.
questions.modelAnswer: All protrude except temporalis retracts; All elevate except lateral pterygoid depresses; Medial & lateral pterygoid produce side‑to‑side movement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lateral relations of lateral pterygoid:
questions.explanation: Structures lateral to the lateral pterygoid include the ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid venous plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral relations of lateral pterygoid: mandible, medial pterygoid, temporalis tendon, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus.
questions.modelAnswer: Ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial relations of lateral pterygoid:
questions.explanation: Medial to the lateral pterygoid lie the deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palati muscle, middle meningeal artery, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, and sphenomandibular ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Medial relations of lateral pterygoid: medial pterygoid, tensor palati, MMA, V3 trunk, otic ganglion.
questions.modelAnswer: Deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palati, MMA, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, sphenomandibular ligament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 ligaments of TMJ:
questions.explanation: The three ligaments associated with the TMJ are the lateral ligament (thickening of joint capsule), stylomandibular ligament (from styloid to mandible), and sphenomandibular ligament (from spine to lingula).
questions.keyConcept: TMJ ligaments: lateral, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of posterior division of mandibular nerve:
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the mandibular nerve gives three branches: auriculotemporal (sensory to temple and ear), lingual (sensory to anterior two-thirds of tongue), and inferior alveolar (sensory to lower teeth and chin).
questions.keyConcept: Posterior V3 branches: auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.
questions.modelAnswer: Auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of inferior alveolar nerve:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives off the mylohyoid branch before entering the mandibular foramen, then continues as the mental nerve (exiting mental foramen) and incisive nerve (supplying lower anterior teeth).
questions.keyConcept: Inferior alveolar branches: mylohyoid, mental, incisive nerves.
questions.modelAnswer: Mylohyoid, mental, incisive.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 4 branches of maxillary nerve:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off a meningeal branch, two ganglionic branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion, the zygomatic nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve branches: meningeal, two ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal, two ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of pterygopalatine fossa:
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa is bounded anteriorly by the posterior maxilla, posteriorly by the pterygoid process, medially by the palatine bone, and laterally it opens into the infratemporal fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa: maxilla anterior, pterygoid posterior, palatine medial, open laterally.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: posterior maxilla; Posterior: pterygoid process; Medial: palatine bone; Lateral: opens to infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Contents of pterygopalatine fossa:
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa contains the third part of the maxillary artery, branches of the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion with associated autonomic connections.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa contents: maxillary artery part 3, maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion.
questions.modelAnswer: 3rd part of maxillary artery, maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of 3rd part of maxillary artery:
questions.explanation: The third (pterygopalatine) part of the maxillary artery gives posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater and lesser palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal branches, and the artery of the pterygoid canal.
questions.keyConcept: Third maxillary artery: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, pterygoid canal.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater & lesser palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, artery of pterygoid canal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Drainage of pterygoid plexus:
questions.explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus drains into the maxillary vein, which then joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein, ultimately connecting to the external jugular system.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus drains to maxillary vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Maxillary vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Communications of pterygoid plexus:
questions.explanation: The pterygoid plexus communicates with the facial vein via the deep facial vein, with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins through foramen ovale and spinosum, and with the inferior ophthalmic vein.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus: facial vein, cavernous sinus, inferior ophthalmic vein connections.
questions.modelAnswer: Facial vein (deep facial), cavernous sinus (emissary veins), inferior ophthalmic vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Otic ganglion:
questions.explanation: The otic ganglion sits below the foramen ovale; its parasympathetic root comes from the inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic branch of CN IX, tympanic plexus, and lesser petrosal nerve; it distributes to the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Otic ganglion: below foramen ovale; parasympathetic from inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic plexus to parotid.
questions.modelAnswer: Site: below foramen ovale; Sympathetic root: around MMA; Parasympathetic root: inferior salivatory nucleus → tympanic branch of 9 → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion; Distribution: postganglionic to parotid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Compare sympathetic root:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic roots differ by ganglion: otic ganglion receives fibers around the middle meningeal artery, submandibular ganglion around the facial artery, and sphenopalatine ganglion around the internal carotid artery via the deep petrosal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic roots: otic (MMA), submandibular (facial artery), sphenopalatine (ICA/deep petrosal).
questions.modelAnswer: Otic: around MMA; Submandibular: around facial artery; Sphenopalatine: around ICA (deep petrosal).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tributaries of external jugular vein:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein receives tributaries including the anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular veins, draining superficial structures of the head and neck.
questions.keyConcept: EJV tributaries: anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Floor of posterior triangle:
questions.explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius, and scalenus anterior muscles, from superficial to deep.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior triangle floor: semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius and anterior.
questions.modelAnswer: Semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius, scalenus anterior.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 5 contents of posterior triangle:
questions.explanation: Five important contents of the posterior triangle are the spinal accessory nerve, roots and trunks of the brachial plexus, cutaneous nerves of the cervical plexus, subclavian vein, and external jugular vein.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior triangle contents: spinal accessory, brachial plexus roots/trunks, cervical plexus cutaneous, subclavian vein, EJV.
questions.modelAnswer: Spinal accessory nerve, roots/trunks of brachial plexus, cutaneous nerves of cervical plexus, subclavian vein, external jugular vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cutaneous branches of cervical plexus:
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus cutaneous branches are the great auricular (C2-3 to ear and parotid), lesser occipital (C2 to lateral scalp), transverse cervical (C2-3 to lateral neck), and supraclavicular nerves (C3-4 to shoulder and chest).
questions.keyConcept: Cervical plexus: great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical, supraclavicular nerves.
questions.modelAnswer: Great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical, supraclavicular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of anterior triangle:
questions.explanation: The anterior triangle is bounded anteriorly by the anterior median line of the neck, posteriorly by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, and superiorly by the inferior border of the mandible and line extending to the mastoid process.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior triangle: midline anterior, sternomastoid posterior, mandible/mastoid line superior.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: anterior median line; Posterior: anterior border of sternomastoid; Superior: inferior border of mandible and line to mastoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of submental triangle:
questions.explanation: The submental triangle has its apex at the symphysis menti, sides formed by the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles, base along the body of hyoid, and floor formed by the mylohyoid muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Submental triangle: apex symphysis menti, sides anterior bellies of digastric, base hyoid body, floor mylohyoid.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex: symphysis menti; Sides: anterior bellies of digastric; Base: body of hyoid; Floor: mylohyoid muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Contents of submental triangle:
questions.explanation: Contents of the submental triangle include the submental lymph nodes, submental artery and vein, mylohyoid nerve and vessels, and small veins that contribute to the anterior jugular vein formation.
questions.keyConcept: Submental contents: submental nodes, vessels, mylohyoid nerve and vessels, veins to anterior jugular.
questions.modelAnswer: Submental lymph nodes, submental artery and vein, mylohyoid nerve and vessels, small veins forming anterior jugular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of digastric triangle:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle boundaries are: anterior belly of digastric, posterior belly of digastric with stylohyoid, and the inferior border of mandible to mastoid; the floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle: anterior/posterior bellies of digastric, mandible to mastoid; floor mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: anterior belly of digastric; Posterior: posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid; Superior: inferior border of mandible to mastoid; Roof: skin, superficial, deep fascia; Floor: mylohyoid and hyoglossus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 5 contents of digastric triangle:
questions.explanation: Five contents of the digastric triangle are the submandibular gland, submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion (parasympathetic), facial artery, and facial vein.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle contents: submandibular gland, LN, ganglion, facial artery and vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Submandibular gland, submandibular LN, submandibular ganglion, facial artery, facial vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of carotid triangle:
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded superiorly by the posterior belly of digastric, anteriorly by the superior belly of omohyoid, posteriorly by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid; the floor is formed by hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors.
questions.keyConcept: Carotid triangle: posterior digastric superior, omohyoid anterior, SCM posterior; floor hyoglossus and constrictors.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: posterior belly of digastric; Anterior: superior belly of omohyoid; Posterior: anterior border of sternomastoid; Roof: skin, fascia; Floor: hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, middle and inferior constrictors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 contents of carotid triangle:
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle contains the common carotid artery and its bifurcation into the internal and external carotid arteries, along with the carotid body (chemoreceptor) and carotid sinus (baroreceptor).
questions.keyConcept: Carotid triangle contains: CCA, ICA, ECA, carotid body and sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: CCA, ICA, ECA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Contents of muscular triangle:
questions.explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid (strap) muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid, which stabilize the larynx and hyoid during swallowing and speech.
questions.keyConcept: Muscular triangle contains infrahyoid strap muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Infrahyoid muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve supply of infrahyoid muscles:
questions.explanation: All infrahyoid muscles are supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-3), except the thyrohyoid which receives C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve, reflecting their developmental origin from cervical somites.
questions.keyConcept: Infrahyoid muscles: all by ansa cervicalis except thyrohyoid (C1 via hypoglossal).
questions.modelAnswer: All by ansa cervicalis except thyrohyoid (C1 via hypoglossal).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve supply of suprahyoid muscles:
questions.explanation: Suprahyoid muscles have varied innervation: mylohyoid and anterior digastric by V3 (nerve to mylohyoid), posterior digastric and stylohyoid by CN VII, and geniohyoid by C1 traveling with the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Suprahyoid: mylohyoid/anterior digastric (V3), posterior digastric/stylohyoid (CN VII), geniohyoid (C1).
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior digastric and mylohyoid by nerve to mylohyoid; Posterior digastric and stylohyoid by facial; Geniohyoid by C1 via hypoglossal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Structure of ansa cervicalis:
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis is a loop of nerve fibers formed by the superior limb (C1 fibers traveling with the hypoglossal) and inferior limb (C2-3 fibers descending from the cervical plexus), supplying infrahyoid muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis: superior limb (C1 via hypoglossal) and inferior limb (C2-3 from plexus).
questions.modelAnswer: Two limbs: superior (C1) and inferior (C2-3).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cervical sympathetic ganglia sites:
questions.explanation: The three paired cervical sympathetic ganglia are positioned at specific vertebral levels: superior ganglion at C2-3, middle ganglion at C6-7, and inferior ganglion (often fused with T1 as stellate ganglion) at C7 level.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical sympathetic ganglia: superior (C2-3), middle (C6-7), inferior (C7).
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: C2-3; Middle: C6-7; Inferior: C7.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of glossopharyngeal nerve:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) gives six branches: tympanic (to middle ear), carotid (to carotid body/sinus), pharyngeal (to pharynx), muscular (to stylopharyngeus), tonsillar, and lingual branches.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar, lingual.
questions.modelAnswer: Tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar, lingual.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of vagus from superior vagal ganglion:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve's superior (jugular) ganglion gives off only meningeal and auricular branches before the nerve descends, contributing to sensory innervation of the dura and external ear.
questions.keyConcept: Superior vagal ganglion branches: meningeal and auricular.
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal, auricular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a common microscopic feature between muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ?
questions.explanation: Both muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs are encapsulated receptors with connective tissue capsules surrounding their sensory endings, distinguishing them from free nerve endings.
questions.keyConcept: Both muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ are encapsulated receptors.
options: They are both present in series with extrafusal fibres.
They both respond only to active contraction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the condition of unilateral inattention (neglect)?
questions.explanation: Unilateral neglect syndrome involves ignoring stimuli from the contralateral side, often manifesting as failure to dress or groom that side, typically caused by right parietal lobe lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Neglect: ignoring contralateral stimuli, often with dressing/grooming deficits on that side.
options: Loss of all sensation on one side of the body
Ignoring stimuli from the opposite side, often with failure to dress or shave that side
Loss of proprioception with preserved touch

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The pterion is a clinically important landmark because it overlies the:
questions.explanation: The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, making it a critical landmark as fractures here can cause epidural hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
options: Anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of the cervical level of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The cervical spinal cord has the largest white matter-to-grey matter ratio among spinal cord levels because it contains the most descending and ascending fiber tracts connecting the brain to all body regions.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio.
options: Has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio
Contains the central canal in a ventral position

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The first order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is located in:
questions.explanation: Proprioception from the lower body is carried by first-order neurons whose cell bodies are located in the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia, where peripheral receptors from muscle spindles and tendon organs synapse.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first-order neuron: spinal (dorsal root) ganglia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The second order neuron for pain and temperature from the face is located in the:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature sensation from the face is carried by the trigeminal nerve to the spinal nucleus of V (caudal part), which is the second-order neuron for this pathway before crossing to the contralateral side.
questions.keyConcept: Pain/temperature from face: second-order neuron in spinal nucleus of V.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tract carries unconscious proprioception from the lower limb to the cerebellum without crossing?
questions.explanation: The posterior spinocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioceptive information from the lower limb directly to the cerebellum on the same side without crossing, originating from Clarke's nucleus at T1-L2.
questions.keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception from lower limb: posterior spinocerebellar tract, uncrossed.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has difficulty initiating movement, resting tremor, and cogwheel rigidity. Which structure is primarily affected?
questions.explanation: Parkinsonism features (difficulty initiating movement, resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity) result from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonism: substantia nigra degeneration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In a complete spinal cord transection at the level of T6, which of the following would be expected?
questions.explanation: A complete transection at T6 would cause paraplegia (paralysis of both lower limbs) since this level is below the cervical region and does not affect upper limb innervation or respiratory muscles.
questions.keyConcept: T6 transection: paraplegia of both lower limbs.
options: Loss of pain sensation from the upper limbs

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries which sensations?
questions.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensation after crossing in the spinal cord, while fine touch and vibration are carried by the dorsal columns.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral spinothalamic tract: pain and temperature.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a component of the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier consists of tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells, a thick basement membrane, and astrocytic end-feet that together restrict molecular passage.
questions.keyConcept: Blood-brain barrier: tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve belongs to which column of cranial nerve nuclei?
questions.explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is a special visceral efferent (SVE) nucleus, innervating muscles derived from the first pharyngeal arch (muscles of mastication).
questions.keyConcept: Motor nucleus of V is special visceral efferent (SVE).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from Clarke's nucleus (nucleus dorsalis) located in the intermediate grey matter at T1-L2 levels, carrying proprioceptive information to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from Clarke's nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a rapid, monosynaptic reflex that helps maintain muscle length?
questions.explanation: The stretch (myotatic) reflex is a monosynaptic reflex mediated by muscle spindles that detects changes in muscle length and rapidly adjusts muscle tone to maintain posture.
questions.keyConcept: Stretch reflex: monosynaptic reflex maintaining muscle length.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with syringomyelia typically loses pain and temperature sensation in the upper limbs but retains touch and vibration. Which tract is damaged?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia damages the crossing fibers of the lateral spinothalamic tract in the cervical region, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature while preserving dorsal column functions like touch and vibration.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia: lateral spinothalamic tract damaged, losing pain/temperature but preserving touch/vibration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe)?
questions.explanation: The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) receives vestibular input and controls balance, posture, and eye movements, making it essential for spatial orientation.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibulocerebellum: controls balance and eye movements.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The corticospinal tract in the spinal cord is located in which funiculus?
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract is located primarily in the lateral funiculus (about 85% of fibers), with the remaining fibers traveling in the anterior funiculus as the anterior corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal tract: mainly lateral funiculus, some in anterior funiculus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure is part of the diencephalon?
questions.explanation: The diencephalon consists of four major structures: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (including pineal gland), and subthalamus, surrounding the third ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Diencephalon: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lesion of the left optic tract causes:
questions.explanation: A left optic tract lesion causes right homonymous hemianopia because optic tract fibers carry information from the contralateral visual field, so damage affects the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Left optic tract lesion: right homonymous hemianopia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia modulate movement through indirect and direct pathways that influence thalamic output to the motor cortex, without directly executing voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia: modulate movement and motor learning, not direct execution.
options: Modulation of movement and motor learning

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the:
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), arising from the inferior (recurrent) laryngeal branch that loops under the aortic arch on the left and subclavian artery on the right.
questions.keyConcept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve: branch of vagus nerve (CN X).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the extrapyramidal tracts?
questions.explanation: Extrapyramidal tracts (rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal) influence muscle tone, posture, and automatic movements rather than fine skilled movements controlled by the pyramidal system.
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts: regulate posture and muscle tone.
options: They originate exclusively from the motor cortex.
They are concerned with fine skilled movements.
They influence posture and muscle tone.
They decussate only in the medulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cauda equina is composed of:
questions.explanation: The cauda equina (horse's tail) consists of the dorsal and ventral roots of the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal spinal nerves traveling within the subarachnoid space below L1-2.
questions.keyConcept: Cauda equina: dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral, coccygeal nerves.
options: The lower part of the spinal cord
Dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerves

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve is responsible for the sensory innervation of the lower eyelid?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of V2) provides sensory innervation to the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, entering through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid sensory innervation: infraorbital nerve (V2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The maxillary nerve exits the skull through which foramen?
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) exits the skull through the foramen rotundum, passing from the middle cranial fossa into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve exits via foramen rotundum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The optic nerve is a derivative of the:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve develops as an outpouching of the diencephalon (forerain), making it technically a CNS tract rather than a true peripheral nerve, with myelin provided by oligodendrocytes.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve is a diencephalon derivative, not true peripheral nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the arachnoid granulations?
questions.explanation: Arachnoid granulations (Pacchionian bodies) are herniations of arachnoid mater into dural venous sinuses that absorb cerebrospinal fluid into the venous system.
questions.keyConcept: Arachnoid granulations absorb CSF into venous sinuses.
options: They absorb cerebrospinal fluid into the venous system.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the medulla oblongata, receiving input from the spinal cord and cerebral cortex and sending climbing fiber projections to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary nucleus: located in medulla oblongata.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has weakness of the right lower face, but can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Preserved forehead wrinkling indicates intact upper motor neuron (UMN) innervation to the facial nucleus's upper face region; weakness of only the lower face indicates a UMN lesion affecting the contralateral corticobulbar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Lower face weakness with spared forehead: contralateral corticobulbar (UMN) lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The muscle spindle is stretched by contraction of which fibres?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within the spindle, and when activated, they contract these fibers, stretching the sensory region and increasing spindle sensitivity to muscle stretch.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons stretch intrafusal fibers, increasing muscle spindle sensitivity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the gate control theory of pain?
questions.explanation: The gate control theory proposes that large myelinated afferent fibers (touch) can inhibit transmission of pain signals in the dorsal horn through interneurons, effectively 'closing the gate' on pain perception.
questions.keyConcept: Gate control: large afferent fiber activity inhibits dorsal horn pain transmission.
options: Pain is transmitted only by large myelinated fibres.
Activity in large afferent fibres can inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
Pain is solely a cortical phenomenon.
Endorphins are released only from the pituitary.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The medial geniculate body is part of the auditory pathway and receives input from the:
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus, serving as the thalamic relay for the auditory pathway to the auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body receives input from inferior colliculus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with a tumour in the left frontal eye field (area 8) will have difficulty:
questions.explanation: The left frontal eye field (area 8) controls conjugate gaze to the right by sending signals that move both eyes rightward; a lesion here causes difficulty gazing to the contralateral (right) side.
questions.keyConcept: Left frontal eye field controls gaze to the right (contralateral).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the prefrontal cortex?
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex mediates executive functions including planning, decision-making, personality expression, and social behavior, distinguishing humans from other primates.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal cortex: executive functions and personality.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The choroid plexus is present in all ventricles except:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct (connecting third and fourth ventricles) is a narrow channel lined with ependyma but lacks choroid plexus, making it distinct from all three ventricles which have choroid plexus for CSF production.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct lacks choroid plexus (only ventricles have it).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the spinal cord at levels:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord from T1 to L2 levels, representing the thoracolumbar outflow of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons: T1-L2 (thoracolumbar outflow).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue except the:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus, which is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus via the vagus nerve (CN X) due to its origin from the fourth pharyngeal arch.
questions.keyConcept: Palatoglossus is supplied by vagus (CN X), not hypoglossal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a pure motor cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is a pure motor nerve carrying general somatic efferent fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, with no sensory component.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is pure motor to tongue muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) coordinates movements between which structures?
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) connects the vestibular nuclei to the abducens and oculomotor nuclei, coordinating eye movements with head movements in the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
questions.keyConcept: MLF coordinates eyes and head via vestibulo-ocular reflex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The limbic system, including the hippocampus, amygdala, and cingulate gyrus, is fundamentally involved in emotional processing and memory formation, particularly through connections with the hypothalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic system: emotion and memory processing.
options: It is involved in emotion and memory.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has loss of pain and temperature on the right side of the body and loss of proprioception on the left side below the level of a spinal cord lesion. This pattern is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: This pattern describes Brown-Sequard syndrome: ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss (corticospinal and dorsal columns) below the lesion with contralateral pain/temperature loss (lateral spinothalamic crossing fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral motor and proprioception loss, contralateral pain loss below lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A tumor in the floor of the fourth ventricle (facial colliculus region) most directly damages which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus in the floor of the 4th ventricle overlies the abducent (CN VI) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: facial nerve wraps around abducens nucleus in floor of fourth ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects:
questions.explanation: The aqueduct links the 3rd and 4th ventricles through the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct connects third ventricle to fourth ventricle.
options: Fourth ventricle and the subarachnoid space

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fourth ventricle communicates with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture, the:
questions.explanation: The median aperture (foramen of Magendie) drains CSF into the cisterna magna.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle communicates with subarachnoid space via lateral apertures of Luschka and median aperture of Magendie.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient develops contralateral loss of pain and temperature of the body with ipsilateral facial signs. The occluded vessel is the:
questions.explanation: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral pain and temperature loss below lesion: lateral spinothalamic tract lesion.
options: Superior cerebellar artery supplying the upper cerebellum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Contralateral sensation from the face and body is represented in the:
questions.explanation: SI (areas 3,1,2) maps the contralateral half of the body and face.
questions.keyConcept: Face represented upside down in somatosensory cortex, with larger areas for lips and fingers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The motor branch to mylohyoid arises from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve as the:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives the (motor) nerve to mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Motor branch to mylohyoid arises from posterior division of mandibular nerve (V3).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tract is the main alternative (indirect) pathway to the corticospinal tract for motor control?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus/rubrospinal tract is the principal alternative motor pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract: main indirect pathway from cerebellum via red nucleus to spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The first-order neuron carrying pain and temperature from the face lies in the:
questions.explanation: Cell bodies are in the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Pain and temperature first-order neuron: pseudounipolar cell body in trigeminal ganglion.
options: Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The primary motor cortex (area 4) is chiefly responsible for:
questions.explanation: Area 4 executes movement; planning is premotor/SMA.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex (area 4): execution of voluntary movement.
options: Sensory perception of limb position in space
Converting the plan into actual movement

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lesion of the spinal accessory nerve causes paralysis of:
questions.explanation: CN XI supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal accessory nerve: sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The genu of the corpus callosum is supplied mainly by the:
questions.explanation: The ACA supplies the genu of the corpus callosum.
questions.keyConcept: Genu of corpus callosum supplied by anterior cerebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: On the medial surface of the infratemporal fossa lies the:
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid muscle lies on medial surface of infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The supplementary motor area is located in the:
questions.explanation: The SMA lies on the medial frontal gyrus, anterior to the leg area.
questions.keyConcept: Supplementary motor area located in medial aspect of frontal lobe (medial area 6).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Broca's motor speech area lies in the:
questions.explanation: Broca's area = pars opercularis/triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Brocas motor speech area in inferior frontal gyrus (dominant hemisphere).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The chief retractor of the mandible is the:
questions.explanation: Posterior temporalis fibers retract the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis is the chief retractor of mandible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The sensory (dorsal) part of the spinal cord develops from the:
questions.explanation: The alar plate forms sensory (dorsal) grey matter.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory dorsal horn develops from alar lamina of neural tube.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Unconscious proprioception from the upper limb (elbow/wrist) is carried by the:
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
