questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from upper limb to cerebellum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient shows ipsilateral tongue atrophy, contralateral loss of vibration, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature of the body. The lesion is in the:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (CN XII, medial lemniscus, pyramid).
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviation toward lesion with ipsilateral atrophy: hypoglossal nerve lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tract passes through the superior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: The anterior spinocerebellar tract enters via the SCP.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle carries dentatothalamic fibers from cerebellum to thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cavernous sinus thrombosis from a "danger area" facial infection spreads via the:
questions.explanation: Facial vein to superior ophthalmic vein to cavernous sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial infection: danger area around nose/upper lip.
options: Inferior petrosal sinus to the IJV

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of chemical synapse?
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are sensitive to drugs because neurotransmitter synthesis, release, and receptor binding can be pharmacologically modified, unlike electrical synapses which have no synaptic delay or neurotransmitter involvement.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses are sensitive to drugs modifying neurotransmitter pathways.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Concerning chemical synapses, all the followings are true, Except:
questions.explanation: Chemical synapse transmission typically has a delay of only 0.3-0.5 msec (not 3-5 msec) due to the rapid release, diffusion, and receptor activation process at the synapse.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapse delay is 0.3-0.5 msec, not 3-5 msec.
options: It constitutes the majority in human being.
It may be excitatory or inhibitory.
Conduction of action potential is unidirectional.
The delay of transmission is 3-5 msec.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: For cells that communicate by electrical synapses, the message travels between cells via:
questions.explanation: Electrical synapses transmit signals through gap junctions (connexons) that allow direct ionic current flow between cells, enabling nearly instantaneous bidirectional communication.
questions.keyConcept: Electrical synapses use gap junctions for direct ionic current flow between cells.
options: Ions moving across the synaptic cleft.
Active transport across the synaptic cleft.
Passive transport across the synaptic cleft.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Excitatory postsynaptic potential can be mediated by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) are generated when sodium channels open, allowing Na+ influx that depolarizes the neuron toward threshold for action potential firing.
questions.keyConcept: EPSP mediated by opening of Na+ channels.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Opening of ligand-gated Cl- channels causes:
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated chloride channels (as in GABA-A receptors) increase Cl- conductance, causing hyperpolarization that makes the neuron less likely to fire, resulting in postsynaptic inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Opening of ligand-gated Cl- channels causes inhibition (hyperpolarization).
options: No change in resting membrane potential.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The binding of a neurotransmitter to its receptor at an inhibitory synapse can lead to the ______ of ______ channels.
questions.explanation: At inhibitory synapses, neurotransmitter binding opens potassium channels, allowing K+ efflux that hyperpolarizes the neuron and reduces neuronal excitability.
questions.keyConcept: Inhibitory synapse: opening of potassium channels.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following factors depress synaptic transmission?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia depresses synaptic transmission by impairing the energy-dependent processes required for neurotransmitter synthesis, vesicle packaging, and the Na+/K+ ATPase maintaining membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoxia depresses synaptic transmission by impairing energy-dependent processes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Synaptic delay is:
questions.explanation: Synaptic delay refers to the minimal time (approximately 0.5 msec) required for neurotransmitter release, diffusion across the cleft, and receptor activation at a chemical synapse.
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic delay is approximately 0.5 milliseconds in CNS.
options: The time needed for release of neurotransmitter from synaptic vesicles.
The minimal delay time in the central nervous system is about 0.5 millisecond.
Determined by the type of the neurotransmitter.
Determined by the number of postsynaptic receptors.
The time needed for breakdown of neurotransmitter.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Synaptic fatigue is due to:
questions.explanation: Synaptic fatigue results when neurotransmitter release rate exceeds synthesis rate, depleting readily available vesicles and causing transmission failure with sustained stimulation.
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic fatigue: imbalance between synthesis and release rates depletes vesicles.
options: Inability to release neurotransmitters by exocytosis.
Failure of action potentials to open voltage-gated Ca++ channels.
Imbalance between rates of synthesis and release of neurotransmitters.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A prolonged output discharge could be obtained from which of the following processing way?
questions.explanation: A reverberating circuit allows signals to persist by feedback loops where outputs circle back through interneurons to the original neurons, producing prolonged discharge even after the stimulus ceases.
questions.keyConcept: Reverberating circuit produces prolonged output discharge via feedback loops.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The after discharge in a neuronal pool is based mainly upon the:
questions.explanation: After discharge occurs through reverberatory circuits that maintain neuron firing through positive feedback loops, extending the response beyond the initial stimulus duration.
questions.keyConcept: After discharge: reverberatory circuits maintain firing beyond stimulus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following refers to one presynaptic neuron terminating on many postsynaptic neurons?
questions.explanation: Divergence occurs when one presynaptic neuron branches to terminate on many postsynaptic neurons, allowing amplification and spread of neural signals throughout the nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Divergence: one presynaptic neuron connects to many postsynaptic neurons.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Receptor potential is characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Receptor potentials are graded potentials whose amplitude increases proportionally with stimulus intensity, unlike action potentials which follow the all-or-none law.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor potential intensity increases with stimulus intensity (graded, not all-or-none).
options: Its intensity is increased by increase intensity of stimulation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Regarding neurotransmitters:
questions.explanation: Dopamine functions as a mood-modulating neurotransmitter; reduced dopamine activity is associated with depression while excess is linked to schizophrenia.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine function is related to mood.
options: Dopamine function is related to mood.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that increases the permeability of Postsynaptic neuron to:
questions.explanation: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting by increasing chloride ion permeability through GABA-A receptors.
questions.keyConcept: GABA increases Cl- permeability causing inhibition.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Concerning sensory receptors, all the followings are true, Except:
questions.explanation: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily (unlike many other excitable tissues); they maintain responsiveness during sustained stimulation, though they may adapt at different rates.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following receptors are phasic receptors Except:
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are tonic (slowly adapting) receptors that continue firing during sustained stimulation, unlike phasic receptors like Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner's corpuscles, hair end organs, and Merkel's discs which adapt rapidly.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings are tonic receptors; others listed are phasic.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Specificity:
questions.explanation: Specificity refers to each receptor's selective sensitivity to one particular form of energy (its adequate stimulus), such as light for photoreceptors or pressure for mechanoreceptors.
questions.keyConcept: Specificity: each receptor most sensitive to its adequate stimulus.
options: Is a state of partial depolarization.
Is due to high intensity of the stimulus.
Means that each receptor is most sensitive to a specific form of energy called Adequate stimulus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Pain produced by tissue damage is due to release of:
questions.explanation: Tissue damage releases kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) which sensitize nociceptors, causing pain as part of the inflammatory response to injury.
questions.keyConcept: Pain from tissue damage: release of kinins (bradykinin).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The fast pain sensation that accompanies a painful trauma is carried to C.N.S. by fibers that belong to:
questions.explanation: Fast pain (first pain) is carried by A-delta fibers (type II), which are thinly myelinated for rapid conduction of sharp, well-localized pain signals.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain: carried by A-delta fibers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Slow pain:
questions.explanation: Slow pain is transmitted by unmyelinated C fibers to non-specific thalamic nuclei, perceived diffusely in the sensory cortex, and produces dull, poorly localized, prolonged pain.
questions.keyConcept: Slow pain: C fibers, non-specific thalamic nuclei, diffuse perception.
options: Is carried along type A-delta fibers.
Pathway activates the non-specific thalamic nuclei.
Is perceived mainly in sensory cortex.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Concerning referred pain:
questions.explanation: Referred pain is pain perceived in somatic structures distant from the diseased viscus, occurring when visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal segments.
questions.keyConcept: Referred pain: visceral pain perceived in somatic area sharing same dorsal root level.
options: It is felt in the somatic structure innervated by different dorsal root from that innervating the diseased viscus.
It can’t be explained by convergence projection theory.
It can’t be explained by convergence facilitation theory.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Concerning headache:
questions.explanation: Headache is a form of referred pain where intracranial and extracranial structures refer pain to the head through shared sensory innervation from trigeminal and cervical nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Headache is referred pain from intracranial/extracranial structures.
options: It is an example of referred pain.
It is only caused by intracranial causes.
It is only caused by extracranial causes.
Nausea and vomiting are not symptoms occurring during migraine attack.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Tic douloureux:
questions.explanation: Tic douloureux (trigeminal neuralgia) causes sharp, lancinating facial pain due to trigeminal nerve dysfunction, often triggered by innocuous stimuli like touching the face.
questions.keyConcept: Tic douloureux: sharp lancinating pain in trigeminal distribution.
options: Is due to convergence facilitation theory.
Is due to sensitization of pain receptors by chemicals.
Sharp lancinating pain in the distribution of the facial nerve.
Is an example of secondary hyperalgesia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The analgesia system includes:
questions.explanation: The analgesia system includes the periaqueductal grey matter in the midbrain and the raphe magnus nucleus in the medulla, which modulate pain transmission through descending inhibitory pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Analgesia system: periaqueductal area in midbrain, raphe magnus in medulla.
options: Raphe magnus nucleus in the post horn of the spinal cord.
The peri-aqueductal area in the mid-brain.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Pain sensation can be inhibited by:
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation activates descending pain inhibitory pathways from the periaqueductal grey to the dorsal horn, blocking pain signal transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid receptor stimulation inhibits pain sensation.
options: Increasing the pain threshold by kinin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In a neurological examination, while performing cotton wool test:
questions.explanation: The cotton wool test assesses fine touch (discriminative touch) using Meissner's corpuscles and hair follicle receptors that are moderate adaptors, particularly sensitive on glabrous skin like fingertips.
questions.keyConcept: Cotton wool test: fine/discriminative touch via mechanoreceptors (Meissner's corpuscles).
options: The sensation tested is fine touch.
The sensation tested is carried on C fibers only.
The receptors are moderately adapting receptors.
The cotton is felt better on the palmar side of the hands.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Tactile discrimination is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Tactile discrimination (two-point discrimination) uses rapidly adapting receptors like Meissner's corpuscles to detect texture and shape, tested by ability to distinguish two close points.
questions.keyConcept: Tactile discrimination: rapidly adapting sensation tested by two-point discrimination.
options: It is tested through pin prick test.
Perceived at the level of the thalamus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium ions (Na+) rapid influx through voltage-gated channels cause the sharp upstroke of the action potential, taking the membrane potential from -70mV toward +30mV.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ influx causes rapid depolarization phase of action potential.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The resting membrane potential is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential (-70mV) most closely matches K+ equilibrium potential (-90mV) because the membrane is more permeable to K+ at rest through leak channels.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential closest to K+ equilibrium potential.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The following sensation is not perceived by Somatosensory A 1:
A. Crude Touch.
B. Fast pain.
C. Vibration sense.
D. Proprioceptive sensation.
E. Stereognosis.
questions.explanation: Crude touch is transmitted by the anterior spinothalamic tract, not by somatosensory area 1 which processes fine/discriminative touch, vibration, proprioception, and stereognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 does not process crude touch (anterior spinothalamic does).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Regarding somatosensory area 1 all are correct, Except:
A. Lies anterior to central gyrus.
B. Size of representation depends on number of receptors.
C. Have columns that is specialized to receive one type of sensation.
D. Contralateral representation.
E. Share in pyramidal tract origin.
questions.explanation: Somatosensory area 1 lies posterior to the central gyrus (postcentral gyrus), not anterior; it receives contralateral input, has columns specialized for single sensation types, and its representation size reflects receptor density.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 lies posterior to central gyrus (postcentral gyrus).
options: Size of representation depends on number of receptors
Have columns that is specialized to receive one type of sensation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Muscle stretch reflex is facilitated by:
A. Medullary reticular formation
B. Cortical area 4
C. Red nucleus
D. Cortical area 6
E. Lentiform nucleus of basal ganglia
questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex (area 4) facilitates the muscle stretch reflex through corticospinal influences on gamma motor neurons that regulate muscle spindle sensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Cortical area 4 facilitates stretch reflex via corticospinal influence on gamma neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
If the gamma efferent discharge to a muscle is sectioned, what you expect to happen:
A. The muscle will be paralyzed.
B. Increased muscle spindle sensitivity
C. Energy consumption by brain is the same.
D. Ability to carry a load is affected.
E. Tone of the muscle is not affected.
questions.explanation: Sectioning gamma efferents reduces spindle sensitivity, impairing load detection and the ability to make automatic adjustments during weight-bearing activities.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma efferent sectioning: reduced load-carrying ability due to loss of spindle sensitivity.
options: Energy consumption by brain is the same
Ability to carry a load is affected
Tone of the muscle is not affected

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
When you passively and slowly stretch a muscle, which of the following afferent fiber will continue to discharge:
A. Ia neurons
B. II neurons
C. Ib neurons
D. IIa neurons
E. Y neurons
questions.explanation: Type II (secondary) afferents from nuclear bag and chain fibers in muscle spindles continue firing during slow sustained stretch, unlike rapidly adapting Ia fibers which fire only during changes.
questions.keyConcept: Type II (secondary) afferents fire during slow sustained stretch (non-adapting).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The withdrawal reflex is initiated by stimulation of which of the following receptors?
A. Muscle spindle
B. Joint capsule receptor
C. Cutaneous free nerve ending
D. Golgi tendon organ
E. Pacinian corpuscles
questions.explanation: The withdrawal (flexor) reflex is initiated by cutaneous nociceptors (free nerve endings) detecting painful stimuli, activating flexor muscles to remove the limb from the harmful stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Withdrawal reflex initiated by cutaneous free nerve endings (nociceptors).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
An athlete was carrying a heavy weight during a competition for a time and then he suddenly left it. This could be explained by activation of:
A. IIb fibers
B. Ia fibers
C. Ib fibers
D. Gamma efferent fibers
E. a motor neurons
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs (Ib fibers) detect muscle tension; when tension becomes excessive, they trigger autogenic inhibition to protect the muscle from damage by relaxing it.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organ (Ib fibers): autogenic inhibition when tension excessive.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Reflex contraction of the extensor muscles of the right leg can occur following:
A. Hitting a chair with the left foot.
B. Stretching the flexor muscles in the right leg
C. Stretching of the flexor muscles in left hand
D. Excessive stretch of extensors of the right leg
E. Painful kicking of the right knee.
questions.explanation: The crossed extensor reflex causes the contralateral extensor to contract when a limb is withdrawn from pain, allowing weight shift and postural support while the affected side flexes.
questions.keyConcept: Crossed extensor reflex: contralateral extensor contraction when ipsilateral limb withdrawn from pain.
options: Hitting a chair with the left foot
Stretching the flexor muscles in the right leg
Stretching of the flexor muscles in left hand
Excessive stretch of extensors of the right leg
Painful kicking of the right knee

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The idea of the voluntary movement is generated in which one of the following:
A. 1ry motor area 4
B. Premotor cortex
C. Supplementary motor area
D. Prefrontal cortex
E. Cerebellum
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex generates the idea and plan for voluntary movement, while the primary motor cortex executes the movement and supplementary motor area prepares for it.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal cortex generates the idea of voluntary movement.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
A patient has lesion in right motor area 4, he will have:
A. Loss fine discrete movements in right leg
B. Loss of fine discrete movements in left hand
C. Complete loss of gross movements in right hand
D. Increased muscle tone in right leg
E. Decreased muscle tone in right hand.
questions.explanation: A lesion in the right motor area 4 causes loss of fine discrete movements in the contralateral (left) hand due to the crossed corticospinal tract; this is classic upper motor neuron weakness.
questions.keyConcept: Right motor cortex lesion: loss of fine movements in left hand (contralateral).
options: Loss fine discrete movements in right leg
Loss of fine discrete movements in left hand
Complete loss of gross movements in right hand
Increased muscle tone in right leg
Decreased muscle tone in right hand

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Vascular infarcts involve motor cortex after few weeks will be associated with which of the following:
A. Spastic muscle paralysis
B. Flaccid muscle paralysis
C. No paralysis, only jerky, fast movements
D. Loss of sensation in ipsilateral foot.
E. Loss of sensation in the contralateral foot.
questions.explanation: After vascular infarcts involving motor cortex, spastic muscle paralysis develops over weeks due to loss of upper motor neuron inhibition of spinal reflexes, resulting in hypertonia and hyperreflexia.
questions.keyConcept: Motor cortex infarct: spastic paralysis develops over weeks.
options: No paralysis, only jerky, fast movements
Loss of sensation in ipsilateral foot
Loss of sensation in the contralateral foot

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following is Not characterizing the pyramidal tract?
A. It has only cortical origin.
B. It terminates on AHCs and cranial nerve nuclei.
C. It is functioning since birth.
D. 90% of it cross to opposite side at medulla.
E. It is only one neuron from cortex to AHCs.
questions.explanation: The pyramidal tract is not fully functional at birth (infants have primitive reflexes but lack voluntary control); it matures over the first two years as corticospinal fibers fully develop.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal tract is not fully functional at birth.
options: It terminates on AHCs and cranial nerve nuclei
90% of it cross to opposite side at medulla
It is only one neuron from cortex to AHCs

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The medial motor system includes all the following tracts Except:
A. Vestibulospinal tract
B. Rubrospinal tract
C. Reticulospinal tract
D. Tectospinal tract
E. Ventral corticospinal tract
questions.explanation: The rubrospinal tract belongs to the lateral motor system, not the medial motor system. Medial motor system includes vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal, and ventral corticospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract is part of lateral motor system, not medial.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
In upper motor neuron lesion, there is:
A. Flaccid paralysis
B. No paralysis
C. Spastic muscle
D. Hypotonia
E. Ataxia
questions.explanation: Upper motor neuron lesions cause spastic paralysis with hypertonia and hyperreflexia due to loss of cortical inhibition of spinal reflex arcs, unlike lower motor neuron lesions which cause flaccid paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: UMN lesion: spastic muscle (hypertonia, hyperreflexia).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
In lower motor neuron lesion, loss of superficial reflexes could be explained by the fact that:
A. These reflexes need intact corticospinal tract
B. These reflexes were suppressed by corticospinal tract
C. There is damage to the center of these reflexes
D. There is damage to the afferent of these reflexes
E. There is supraspinal inhibition of these reflexes
questions.explanation: Superficial reflexes (abdominal, cremasteric) are polysynaptic reflexes whose centers are in the spinal cord; LMN damage eliminates the efferent limb of these reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial reflex loss in LMN lesion: damage to reflex center.
options: These reflexes need intact corticospinal tract
These reflexes were suppressed by corticospinal tract
There is damage to the center of these reflexes
There is damage to the afferent of these reflexes
There is supraspinal inhibition of these reflexes

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following nuclei affected in hemiballismus?
A. Caudate nucleus
B. Subthalamic nucleus
C. Substantia nigra
D. Lentiform
E. None of the above
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus is characterized by violent, flinging movements of contralateral limbs resulting from damage to the subthalamic nucleus, disrupting the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Hemiballismus: subthalamic nucleus lesion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The main input of the basal ganglia is to:
A. Caudate
B. Globus pallidus
C. Substantia Nigra
D. Subthalamic nucleus
E. None of the above
questions.explanation: The caudate nucleus (with putamen forming the striatum) is the main input structure of the basal ganglia, receiving excitatory corticostriatal projections and sending output via the globus pallidus.
questions.keyConcept: Main basal ganglia input: caudate nucleus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements concerning the general functional role of the cerebellum is correct?
A. The cerebellum directly stimulates motor neurons required to make a movement
B. The cerebellum is unable to make corrective adjustments to the movement once it is performed
C. The cerebellum does not receive feedback from muscles that execute the actual movement
D. The cerebellum is not involved in the planning of a movement, only its execution
E. The cerebellum plays an active role in the coordination of the muscles required to make a movement
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity during movement through its internal models and predictive control, receiving proprioceptive feedback and making real-time adjustments, but does not directly stimulate motor neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellum coordinates muscles during movement, doesn't directly stimulate motor neurons.
options: The cerebellum directly stimulates motor neurons required to make a movement
The cerebellum is unable to make corrective adjustments to the movement once it is performed
The cerebellum does not receive feedback from muscles that execute the actual movement
The cerebellum is not involved in the planning of a movement, only its execution
The cerebellum plays an active role in the coordination of the muscles required to make a movement

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements best describes a functional role for the cerebellar vermis?
A. Controls and coordinates movements of the axial muscles as well as the shoulder and hip
B. Controls movements that involve distal limb musculature
C. Functions with the cerebral cortex to plan movements
D. Stimulates motor neurons through its connections to the spinal cord
E. Inhibits motor neurons through its connections to the spinal cord
questions.explanation: The cerebellar vermis controls axial and proximal muscles of the shoulders and hips (trunk muscles), while the lateral hemispheres control distal limb musculature for fine movements.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar vermis: axial/proximal muscle control (shoulder, hip).
options: Controls and coordinates movements of the axial muscles as well as the shoulder and hip
Controls movements that involve distal limb musculature
Functions with the cerebral cortex to plan movements
Stimulates motor neurons through its connections to the spinal cord
Inhibits motor neurons through its connections to the spinal cord

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following maneuvers will weakens the stretch reflex in skeletal muscle?
A. Sectioning the dorsal root of a spinal nerve
B. Disruption of the spinocerebellar tract
C. Disruption of the corticospinal tract
D. Sectioning the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side of the skeletal muscle in question
E. Creating a lesion in the contralateral globus pallidus
questions.explanation: Sectioning the dorsal root eliminates the afferent limb of the stretch reflex (Ia fibers from muscle spindles), causing immediate weakening or loss of the reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root sectioning: weakens stretch reflex by cutting afferent limb.
options: Sectioning the dorsal root of a spinal nerve
Sectioning the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side of the skeletal muscle in question
Creating a lesion in the contralateral globus pallidus

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The phenomenon of decerebrate rigidity can be explained, at least in part, by which of the following?
A. Stimulation of type 1b sensory neurons
B. Loss of cerebellar inputs to the red nucleus
C. Overactivity of the medullary reticular nuclei involved in motor control
D. Unopposed activity of the pontine reticular nuclei
E. Degeneration of the nigrostriatal pathway
questions.explanation: Decerebrate rigidity results from loss of pontine reticular nucleus inhibition of medullary reticular nuclei, causing unopposed extensor muscle activity and characteristic rigid posturing.
questions.keyConcept: Decerebrate rigidity: unopposed medullary reticular nuclei activity from pontine loss.
options: Loss of cerebellar inputs to the red nucleus
Overactivity of the medullary reticular nuclei involved in motor control
Unopposed activity of the pontine reticular nuclei

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Excitation of the RAS occurs by:
A. Signals from the sleep centers
B. Analeptic drugs
C. Anesthetics
D. Lack of cortical signals
E. Vascular lesion
questions.explanation: Analeptic drugs (like doxapram) stimulate the reticular activating system by exciting respiratory and vasomotor centers, making them useful in CNS depression.
questions.keyConcept: Analeptic drugs excite the RAS.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
A high school student was trying to solve a math problem. Which of the following is the expected brain EEG waves in this case?
A. Alpha waves
B. Beta waves
C. Theta waves
D. Delta waves
E. Gamma waves
questions.explanation: Gamma waves (30-100 Hz) are associated with high-level cognitive processing and appear during complex problem-solving tasks requiring focused attention.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma waves: present during active problem-solving and cognitive tasks.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
A wife came to the doctor, and complained that her husband talks during his sleep, and that frightens her, the doctor explained that:
A. This is normal in REM sleep
B. She can ask her husband about his dream, and he will probably remember them
C. Teeth grinding is expected to happen
D. She can easily wake him up
E. This probably happens a lot near the morning
questions.explanation: Sleep talking occurs during REM sleep when motor inhibition prevents dream enactment, but the person is difficult to wake from this stage; they typically won't remember the dream.
questions.keyConcept: Sleep talking occurs in REM; difficult to wake, no dream recall.
options: This is normal in REM sleep
She can ask her husband about his dream, and he will probably remember them
Teeth grinding is expected to happen
She can easily wake him up
This probably happens a lot near the morning

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following events are present when we wake up in the morning?
A. Increased activity of anterior hypothalamus and RAS
B. Orexin is in its lowest levels
C. Light activates the pontine reticular formation
D. Norepinephrine and serotonin levels are usually high
E. Acetylcholine promotes wakefulness
questions.explanation: Upon waking, norepinephrine and serotonin levels are high, promoting wakefulness and alertness while orexin (hypocretin) levels rise to maintain arousal.
questions.keyConcept: Waking: high norepinephrine and serotonin, high orexin.
options: Increased activity of anterior hypothalamus and RAS
Orexin is in its lowest levels
Light activates the pontine reticular formation
Norepinephrine and serotonin levels are usually high

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Elaboration of thoughts is considered one of the functions of which of the following areas?
A. Wernicke’s area
B. Parietal cortex
C. Visual association area
D. Prefrontal association area
E. Auditory association area
questions.explanation: The prefrontal association area is responsible for elaborating thoughts, planning, and integrating information from various cortical regions for complex cognitive tasks.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal association area: elaboration of thoughts.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The representational hemisphere is described by which one of the following?
A. It always lies in left hemisphere
B. It has no function
C. It is responsible for visuospatial relations
D. It is concerned with language
E. It contains speech Centre
questions.explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere, usually right, is responsible for visuospatial relationships and perceiving the spatial positions of objects in the environment.
questions.keyConcept: Representational hemisphere: visuospatial relations (usually right).
options: It always lies in left hemisphere
It is responsible for visuospatial relations

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Damage to Broca’s area causes which one of the following?
A. Visual agnosia
B. Paralysis of muscles of pharynx and larynx
C. Limitation of vocabulary to very few words
D. Non understandable excessive words
E. Inattention and neglect
questions.explanation: Broca's aphasia causes non-fluent, effortful speech with limited vocabulary as the patient struggles to motor-plan speech output, though language comprehension remains intact.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's lesion: limited vocabulary, non-fluent but comprehension preserved.
options: Paralysis of muscles of pharynx and larynx
Limitation of vocabulary to very few words

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Anomic aphasia is mostly due to lesion near which of following areas?
A. Angular gyrus
B. Arcuate fasiculus
C. Broca's area
D. Wernicke's area
E. Exner's area
questions.explanation: Anomic aphasia (word-finding difficulty) commonly results from lesions near the angular gyrus, disrupting lexical retrieval while preserving other language functions.
questions.keyConcept: Anomic aphasia: angular gyrus lesion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which one of the followings is concerned with motivation?
A. Wernicke’s area
B. Piriform cortex
C. Prefrontal association area
D. Entorhinal cortex
E. Amygdala
questions.explanation: The amygdala is centrally involved in motivation and emotional processing, particularly fear and reward-related behaviors, through its connections with hypothalamus and brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Amygdala: motivation and emotional processing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The reward center is in which one of the following?
A. Lateral nucleus of hypothalamus
B. Broca's area
C. Cerebellum
D. Red nucleus
E. Arcuate fasciculus
questions.explanation: The reward (pleasure) center is located in the lateral hypothalamus; stimulation produces feelings of satisfaction and reinforces behaviors necessary for survival.
questions.keyConcept: Reward center: lateral hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Stimulation of lateral nucleus of the hypothalamus produces:
A. Fear
B. Bradycardia
C. oxytocin secretion
D. food intake
E. maternal behaviour
questions.explanation: Stimulation of the lateral hypothalamus triggers feeding behavior and food intake (hunger center), while the ventromedial hypothalamus acts as the satiety center.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral hypothalamus stimulation: food intake (hunger).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which area of hypothalamus is responsible for sexual behavior?
A. Supraoptic nucleus
B. Paraventricular nucleus
C. Anterior part of hypothalamus
D. Suprachiasmatic nucleus
E. Pre-optic nucleus
questions.explanation: The anterior hypothalamus contains structures essential for sexual behavior and mating, including the preoptic area which shows sex differences in neuron number.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus: sexual behavior.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The memory of a sequence of events in which a person participated is called:
A. Semantic memory
B. Episodic
C. Implicit
D. Procedural
E. Conditional
questions.explanation: Episodic memory records personal experiences organized in time sequence (autobiographical memory), allowing recall of events in which one actively participated.
questions.keyConcept: Episodic memory: memory of personal events in sequence.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The declarative memory is described by which one of the following?
A. It can be remembered after thinking of related events
B. Recall of general facts is the episodic type
C. Memory of personal experiences is the semantic type
D. Its center is in hippocampus and cerebellum
E. It cannot be converted to non-declarative memory
questions.explanation: Declarative memory can be recalled by thinking of related events; it includes episodic (personal experiences) and semantic (general facts) components, primarily mediated by hippocampus.
questions.keyConcept: Declarative memory: recalled through related events, hippocampal.
options: It can be remembered after thinking of related events
Recall of general facts is the episodic type
Memory of personal experiences is the semantic type
Its center is in hippocampus and cerebellum
It cannot be converted to non-declarative memory

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following describes learning?
A. Memory is not essential for it
B. Sensitization means decreased response to repeated stimuli
C. Operant conditioning is a type of associative learning
D. Habituation and sensitization are types of conditioning learning
E. Habituation means increased response to repeated stimuli
questions.explanation: Operant (instrumental) conditioning is a type of associative learning where behavior is modified by consequences (reward or punishment), distinguishing it from non-associative learning.
questions.keyConcept: Operant conditioning: associative learning via consequences.
options: Memory is not essential for it
Sensitization means decreased response to repeated stimuli
Operant conditioning is a type of associative learning
Habituation and sensitization are types of conditioning learning
Habituation means increased response to repeated stimuli

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Semantic memory is characterized by which of the following?
A. It is the memory of personal events
B. A type of implicit memory
C. It is the memory of facts
D. It is non-declarative memory
E. It is a procedural memory
questions.explanation: Semantic memory is explicit/declarative memory for facts and knowledge about the world (general facts), distinct from episodic memory (personal events) and procedural memory (skills).
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory: memory of facts (general knowledge).
options: It is the memory of personal events
It is the memory of facts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Corticonuclear fibers pass through ……… of internal capsule to reach the brain stem.
questions.explanation: Corticonuclear fibers (corticobulbar tract) pass through the genu (bend) of the internal capsule to reach brainstem cranial nerve nuclei for voluntary control of face and neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Corticonuclear fibers pass through genu of internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Retrolentiform part of internal capsule DOESN'T transmit:
questions.explanation: The retrolentiform part of internal capsule contains visual radiation, occipito-pontine, and parieto-pontine fibers, but the auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part.
questions.keyConcept: Retrolentiform: visual/occipito-parieto-pontine fibers; auditory goes sublentiform.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: UMNL of cranial nerves can result from cerebrovascular accident affecting ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies medial frontal and parietal regions including motor cortex areas controlling lower limbs; CVA here causes contralateral leg weakness and UMN signs.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: UMN lesion of cranial nerves (if affecting cortical areas).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The frontal lobe of cerebral hemisphere DOESN'T include ……… area.
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory area (postcentral gyrus, area 1-3) is in the parietal lobe, not the frontal lobe. Frontal lobe contains premotor, prefrontal, and Broca's areas.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe doesn't include primary somatosensory (it's parietal).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The area of reflex (involuntary) conjugate eye movement lies in ……… lobe of the cerebral hemisphere.
questions.explanation: The occipital lobe contains the area for reflex (involuntary) conjugate eye movements - the visual fixation center in the frontal eye field projects to superior colliculus for reflexive gaze.
questions.keyConcept: Reflex conjugate eye movement area: occipital lobe.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The superior speech center is situated within the ……… area.
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA, medial area 6) is the superior speech center involved in planning and initiating speech movements, lying medial to premotor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Superior speech center: supplementary motor area.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the speech areas:
questions.explanation: Speech areas are typically asymmetric; Broca's and Wernicke's areas are usually dominant in one hemisphere (left in right-handers), not equally present in both.
questions.keyConcept: Speech areas are not present equally in both hemispheres.
options: Motor area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.
Sensory area lies in parietal and temporal lobes.
Sensory area is concerned with understanding visual and auditory information.
Both areas are present in both cerebral hemispheres.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choose the correct statement about the sensory homunculus:
questions.explanation: The sensory homunculus represents the body upside-down (inverted) in the postcentral gyrus, with larger representations for areas with higher receptor density like lips and fingertips.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory homunculus: body represented upside-down in postcentral gyrus.
options: It is the body representation within the motor cortex.
Somatosensory cortex corresponds point by point with regions in ipsilateral side of the body.
The body is represented upside down.
The body representation depends on the size of the target part.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery supplies all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial cerebral surface, orbital inferior surface, and genu of internal capsule, but the anterior limb is supplied by the middle cerebral artery via perforating branches.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery supplies medial surface and genu, not anterior limb of internal capsule.
options: Most of medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere.
Medial aspect of orbital part of inferior surface of the hemisphere.
All anterior limb of internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior choroidal artery is a branch from ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The posterior choroidal artery is a branch of the posterior cerebral artery that supplies the choroid plexus of the lateral and third ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior choroidal artery: branch of posterior cerebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery is responsible for the supply of:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the motor and sensory areas for the contralateral lower limb due to its course along the medial cerebral hemisphere.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: supplies contralateral lower limb motor/sensory areas.
options: Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral upper limb.
Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral lower limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Charcot's artery is the largest branch of ……… set of central branches of circle of Willis.
questions.explanation: Charcot's artery (also called the artery of cerebral hemorrhage) is the largest anterolateral central branch of the circle of Willis, supplying the internal capsule and basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Charcot's artery: largest anterolateral central branch of circle of Willis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Inability to perform tasks although the person has the will to perform it indicates a lesion in ……… area.
questions.explanation: A premotor area lesion causes apraxia - inability to perform tasks despite intact motor pathways and will, due to loss of motor planning programs.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor lesion: apraxia (can't perform tasks despite will).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Inability to recognize familiar objects by touch indicates a lesion in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) results from lesions in the superior parietal lobule, which integrates sensory information for object recognition.
questions.keyConcept: Astereognosis: superior parietal lobule lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Occlusion of right anterior cerebral artery may lead to:
questions.explanation: Right anterior cerebral artery occlusion causes left lower limb paralysis (contralateral) since it supplies the medial motor cortex controlling the leg.
questions.keyConcept: Right ACA occlusion: left lower limb paralysis (contralateral).
options: Paralysis of the left upper limb.
Paralysis of the left lower limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The circle of Willis lies within the ……… subarachnoid cistern.
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis lies within the interpeduncular subarachnoid cistern, surrounding the interpeduncular fossa between the cerebral peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Circle of Willis: lies in interpeduncular subarachnoid cistern.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The floor of the body of the lateral ventricle is formed by all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The floor of the lateral ventricle body is formed by the thalamus, body of caudate nucleus, and body of fornix; the tail of caudate lies in the roof of the inferior horn, not the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Tail of caudate nucleus: in roof of inferior horn, not floor of body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lateral ventricles are connected to the third ventricle via:
questions.explanation: The interventricular foramina of Monro connect each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, allowing CSF flow between these chambers.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral to third ventricle: interventricular foramina of Monro.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choose the correct order of CSF circulation:
questions.explanation: CSF flows from lateral ventricles through interventricular foramina to third ventricle, then through cerebral aqueduct to fourth ventricle, and finally into subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: CSF flow: lateral -> third -> fourth -> subarachnoid space.
options: Third ventricle, lateral ventricles, fourth ventricle, subarachnoid space.
Lateral ventricles, fourth ventricle, third ventricle, central canal.
Lateral ventricles, third ventricle, fourth ventricle, subarachnoid space.
Fourth ventricle, third ventricle, lateral ventricles, central canal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is mesodermal in origin?
questions.explanation: Dura mater is derived from mesoderm (specifically the paraxial mesoderm surrounding the neural tube), while arachnoid and pia mater are ectodermal derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater: mesodermal origin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterior neuropore of neural tube closes at ……… day of pregnancy.
questions.explanation: The anterior neuropore closes at day 25 of embryonic development; failure results in anencephaly. The posterior neuropore closes around day 27.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior neuropore closes at day 25 of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Myelination inside the CNS depends on:
questions.explanation: Myelination in the CNS is performed by oligodendrocytes, which can myelinate multiple axons. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves.
questions.keyConcept: CNS myelination: oligodendrocytes (PNS: Schwann cells).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the development of the spinal cord, choose the incorrect combination:
questions.explanation: The alar lamina (sensory) forms the dorsal horns of grey matter, while the basal lamina (motor) forms the ventral horns - the statement incorrectly matches them.
questions.keyConcept: Alar lamina: dorsal horns; Basal lamina: ventral horns.
options: The lumen of the neural tube – the central canal.
The alar lamina – the ventral horns of the grey matter.
Neurons opposite the sulcus limitans – lateral horns of the grey matter.
The marginal layer – the white matter.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The neural crest gives all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Spinal nerves are formed from dorsal and ventral roots which originate from the neural tube (CNS), not from neural crest. Neural crest gives dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, and postganglionic neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nerves: from neural tube, not neural crest.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Failure of closure of the neural tube leads to:
questions.explanation: Rachischisis (myeloschisis) results from failure of neural tube closure, causing exposure of neural tissue; spina bifida results from vertebral arch defects.
questions.keyConcept: Neural tube closure failure: rachischisis (exposed neural tissue).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The adult derivatives of the telencephalon are:
questions.explanation: The telencephalon develops into the cerebral hemispheres including the basal ganglia, hippocampus, and lateral ventricles, while thalamus, hypothalamus, and midbrain derive from diencephalon and mesencephalon.
questions.keyConcept: Telencephalon: cerebral hemispheres.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cavity of the mesencephalon is:
questions.explanation: The cavity of the mesencephalon is the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius), which connects the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalon cavity: cerebral aqueduct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Protrusion of meninges and brain tissue through a defect in the skull is:
questions.explanation: Meningoencephalocele involves protrusion of both meninges and brain tissue through a skull defect; meningocele involves only meninges.
questions.keyConcept: Meningoencephalocele: meninges and brain tissue protrude through skull defect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match the sign of cerebellar ataxia in column A with its definition in column B.
questions.explanation: Dysmetria is inability to estimate distance during movement; dysdiadochokinesia is inability to perform rapid alternating movements; intention tremor occurs with voluntary movement; nystagmus is rhythmic eye movement.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar signs: dysmetria (distance), dysdiadochokinesia (alternating), intention tremor (movement), nystagmus (eye).

pairs.target: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements.
Shaking of fingers on doing movements.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match the cortical area in column A with the result of lesion in column B.
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area lesion: word comprehension loss; primary auditory: decreased hearing; secondary auditory: sound understanding; frontal eye field: voluntary gaze loss; primary visual: hemianopia with macular sparing.
questions.keyConcept: Lesion effects: Wernicke (comprehension), 1ary auditory (hearing), 2ary auditory (sound meaning), eye field (gaze), 1ary visual (hemianopia).

pairs.target: Inability to understand written or spoken words.
Loss of voluntary conjugate eye movement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The occipitofrontalis muscle accounts for the ……… layer of the scalp.
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle forms the third (musculoaponeurotic) layer of the scalp, connecting the galea aponeurotica to the orbital margins.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis: third layer of scalp.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Hemorrhage reaching the ……… layer of the scalp can cause black eye.
questions.explanation: Blood in the loose areolar tissue layer (subaponeurotic space) of the scalp can track around the orbit producing 'black eye' (periorbital ecchymosis).
questions.keyConcept: Black eye: hemorrhage in loose connective tissue layer of scalp.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Skin of the hairy area of the temple is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) supplies the hairy temple area, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular division.
questions.keyConcept: Hairy temple: auriculotemporal nerve (V3).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The great auricular nerve carries fibers from:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve arises from C2-C3 ventral rami (cervical plexus) and supplies the skin of the ear and adjacent scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve: C2 and C3 ventral rami.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Skin over occipital bone up to the vertex is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The posterior primary rami of C2 and C3 supply the skin over the occipital bone up to the vertex, including the greater and lesser occipital nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital area: supplied by dorsal rami of C2 and C3.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of ……… veins.
questions.explanation: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins at the medial angle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior facial vein: formed by supratrochlear and supraorbital veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The common facial vein drains into the ……… vein.
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein after forming from the facial and anterior facial veins joining.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein: drains into internal jugular vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle covered by deep fascia is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is covered by thebuccal fascia (deep fascia), while orbicularis oculi and oris are covered by superficial fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: covered by deep fascia (buccal fascia).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: Masseter develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication and mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter: first pharyngeal arch derivative.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the orbicularis oculi muscle:
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches behind the lacrimal sac (posterior to it), not in front, to compress and dilate the lacrimal sac.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi lacrimal part: attached behind lacrimal sac.
options: Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its lacrimal part is attached in front of the lacrimal sac.
It develops from the second pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An active muscle during whistling is:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle compresses and purses the lips during whistling, while buccinator muscle keeps food between teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Whistling: orbicularis oris contracts to purse lips.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Accumulation of food in the vestibule of the mouth denotes weakness of ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: Buccinator weakness causes food accumulation in the vestibule because this muscle normally keeps food between the teeth during mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Food in vestibule: buccinator weakness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and lower ear region as part of cervical plexus distribution.
questions.keyConcept: Angle of mandible: great auricular nerve (C2-C3).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pain from the lower eyelid is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) carries pain sensation from the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, exiting through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid pain: infraorbital nerve (V2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Infection in the area of chin leads to enlargement of ……… lymph nodes.
questions.explanation: The submental lymph nodes drain the chin and lower lip midline, lying beneath the chin in the submental triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Chin infection: submental lymph nodes enlarge.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The dural fold which is attached to the skull vault is:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is the dural fold attached to the skull vault along the midline, lying between the cerebral hemispheres with its anterior attachment at the crista galli.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dural fold attached to skull vault.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ethmoidal arteries supply the cranial dura via ……… arteries.
questions.explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from the ophthalmic artery) give off anterior meningeal arteries that supply the cranial dura in the anterior fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Ethmoidal arteries supply dura via anterior meningeal branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following are true about the middle meningeal artery EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through foramen spinosum (not ovale), making it vulnerable to fractures in the temporal region causing epidural hematoma.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery: enters via foramen spinosum, not ovale.
options: It is the largest meningeal artery.
It is a branch from 1st part of maxillary artery.
It enters the cranial cavity through foramen ovale.
It gives frontal and parietal terminal branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An aneurysm of the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery compresses the ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) runs through the cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid artery; an aneurysm here compresses CN VI causing lateral rectus palsy.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous ICA aneurysm compresses abducent nerve (CN VI).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: It is not a must to test the ……… nerve in case of cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) does not pass through the cavernous sinus; it exits via stylomastoid foramen, so it wouldn't be affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve not in cavernous sinus, so not tested in thrombosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cavernous sinus is drained to the transverse sinus by ……… sinus.
questions.explanation: The superior petrosal sinus drains the cavernous sinus into the transverse sinus, running along the petrous ridge at the attachment of tentorium cerebelli.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus drains to transverse sinus via superior petrosal sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the straight sinus:
questions.explanation: The straight sinus deviates to the LEFT to continue as the left transverse sinus (not right); the right transverse sinus typically continues from the superior sagittal sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Straight sinus deviates LEFT to become left transverse sinus.
options: It is formed by union of inferior sagittal sinus and great cerebral vein.
Runs in the junction between falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.
Deviates to the right to continue as the right transverse sinus.
It is connected to the confluence of sinuses.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following diploic veins drains extracranially?
questions.explanation: The frontal diploic vein drains through the supraorbital notch to the supraorbital vein and eventually the angular vein, providing extracranial drainage.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal diploic vein drains extracranially via supraorbital vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the intracranial hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Subdural hemorrhage crosses suture lines because it's venous bleeding with low pressure that accumulates slowly, unlike arterial extradural bleeding which is confined by suture attachments.
questions.keyConcept: Subdural bleeding crosses suture lines (venous).
options: Extradural bleeding means bleeding between dura and arachnoid maters.
Extradural bleeding is commonly venous in origin.
Subdural bleeding is commonly arterial in origin.
Subdural bleeding crosses the suture line.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following are tributaries of external jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein, not the external jugular. The external jugular tributaries are anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains internal jugular, not external jugular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The only tributary of the subclavian vein is:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is the only named tributary of the subclavian vein, carrying blood from the superficial structures of the head and neck.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein: only named tributary of subclavian vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The viscera of the neck are surrounded by ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The pretracheal fascia forms a sheath around the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid gland, fusing laterally with the carotid sheath.
questions.keyConcept: Pretracheal fascia surrounds cervical viscera.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The retropharyngeal space lies:
questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering pharynx/esophagus) anteriorly and prevertebral fascia posteriorly, extending from skull base to T1.
questions.keyConcept: Retropharyngeal space: between buccopharyngeal and prevertebral fascia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The axillary sheath is an extension from ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is an extension of the prevertebral fascia (from the anterior vertebral muscles) that surrounds the axillary vessels and brachial plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Axillary sheath: extension of prevertebral fascia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An infrahyoid muscle supplied directly by C1 ventral ramus is:
questions.explanation: The thyrohyoid muscle is innervated directly by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve, while other infrahyoid muscles receive ansa cervicalis (C1-3).
questions.keyConcept: Thyrohyoid: directly by C1 via hypoglossal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A branch from external carotid artery running in both carotid and digastric triangles is ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The facial artery runs through both carotid triangle (origin from ECA) and digastric triangle (before entering face), giving off branches like submental, superior labial, and lateral nasal.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery: runs through both carotid and digastric triangles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The carotid sheath encloses:
questions.explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve throughout its course in the neck.
questions.keyConcept: Carotid sheath: contains CCA/ICA, IJV, and vagus nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A nerve running along the posterior border of sternomastoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve runs along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle, arising from C2 ventral ramus to supply the scalp behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve: posterior border of SCM.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The subclavian artery is divided into 3 parts by ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: The anterior scalene muscle divides the subclavian artery into three parts: first (posterior to scalene), second (behind scalene), and third (lateral to scalene).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery divided by anterior scalene muscle into 3 parts.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A nerve embedded in the roof of the posterior triangle of the neck and crossing the triangle parallel to levator scapulae is:
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle embedded in its roof, running from the sternocleidomastoid to the trapezius, parallel to levator scapulae.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal accessory nerve: crosses posterior triangle parallel to levator scapulae.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tight scalene muscles can compress:
questions.explanation: Tight scalene muscles (especially anterior and middle) can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus in the costoclavicular space, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Scalene tightness compresses subclavian artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A nerve related to anterior aspect of anterior scalene muscle is:
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve runs on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene muscle, making it vulnerable during scalene blocks and relevant in interscalene anesthesia.
questions.keyConcept: Phrenic nerve: anterior aspect of anterior scalene muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle DOESN'T share in boundaries of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The rectus capitis posterior minor does NOT form boundaries of the suboccipital triangle - only rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, and obliquus capitis inferior do.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle: rectus major, obliquus superior/inferior (NOT rectus minor).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A nerve seen in the floor of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The dorsal ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve) emerges in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, providing motor innervation to suboccipital muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle floor: dorsal ramus of C1.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following lies superficial to temporalis fascia?
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve lies superficial to the temporalis fascia as it ascends toward the temple, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve: superficial to temporalis fascia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle acting as a powerful retractor of the mandible is:
questions.explanation: The temporalis muscle is a powerful retractor of the mandible, pulling the mandibular condyle backward to close the mouth after opening.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis: powerful retractor of mandible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The main opener of the mouth is:
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid is the main mouth opener, pulling the mandibular neck forward and down; gravity and suprahyoid muscles assist.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid: main opener of mouth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The mandibular nerve reaches the infratemporal fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) passes from the middle cranial fossa to the infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve enters infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The trunk of the mandibular nerve supplies ……… muscle(s).
questions.explanation: The trunk of the mandibular nerve gives off medial pterygoid nerve (supplying medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palati) before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions.
questions.keyConcept: V3 trunk supplies: medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, tensor palati.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Middle meningeal artery is encircled by roots of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve encircles the middle meningeal artery with its two roots, forming a neural loop around the vessel in the infratemporal fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve encircles middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Bad extraction of lower 3rd molar tooth may cause loss of sensations from:
questions.explanation: Bad extraction of lower third molar can damage the inferior alveolar nerve (running in the mandibular canal), causing anesthesia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Lower 3rd molar extraction: possible lingual nerve damage (anterior 2/3 tongue).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: To operate on the lower teeth, the ……… nerve is anaesthetized.
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) is anesthetized for lower teeth operations, injected near the mandibular foramen on the medial aspect of the ramus.
questions.keyConcept: Lower teeth surgery: inferior alveolar nerve anesthetized.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A branch from the 3rd part of maxillary artery is:
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar artery is a branch of the third part of maxillary artery that supplies the upper molars and sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior superior alveolar artery: branch of maxillary artery part 3.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A nerve passing between the 2 heads of lateral pterygoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The buccal nerve passes between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle to reach the buccinator muscle, carrying sensory and motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Buccal nerve passes between two heads of lateral pterygoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fracture of neck of mandible can lead to injury of all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve runs on the lateral surface of the mandibular neck, so it can be injured in fractures; the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves are also at risk, but auriculotemporal is not typically affected.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular neck fracture: masseteric, lingual, inferior alveolar nerves at risk.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Maxillary nerve reaches the pterygopalatine fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) passes from the middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve reaches pterygopalatine fossa through foramen rotundum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pain from upper canine teeth is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The upper canine teeth are supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of infraorbital nerve, V2), which also supplies the upper incisors.
questions.keyConcept: Upper canine: anterior superior alveolar nerve (V2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The skin of the prominence of cheek is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the skin over the cheek prominence (zygomatic area), a branch of V2 via the zygomatic nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Cheek prominence: zygomaticotemporal nerve (V2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The facial nerve leaves the cranial cavity by passing through:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the cranial cavity through the stylomastoid foramen located between the styloid and mastoid processes.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve exits via stylomastoid foramen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Facial nerve DOESN'T give parasympathetic supply to ……… gland.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve provides parasympathetic supply to the lacrimal gland via the greater petrosal nerve and to submandibular and sublingual glands via chorda tympani; the parotid gland receives parasympathetic from CN IX.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve doesn't parasympathetically supply parotid gland (CN IX does).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of facial nerve at stylomastoid foramen leads to:
questions.explanation: A lesion at stylomastoid foramen causes lower motor neuron facial paralysis affecting all muscles on that side, including the forehead (loss of frontalis and orbicularis oculi).
questions.keyConcept: Stylomastoid lesion: LMN facial paralysis (entire ipsilateral face).
options: Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral anterior 2/3 of tongue.
Motor loss on the contralateral half of the face.
Motor loss on the ipsilateral half of face.
Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral half of soft palate.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve of pterygoid canal is formed by union of ……… nerves.
questions.explanation: The nerve of pterygoid canal (Vidians nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus).
questions.keyConcept: Nerve of pterygoid canal: greater petrosal + deep petrosal nerves.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Deviation of the uvula to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: Uvula deviation to the right indicates right motor nucleus of vagus (CN X) damage (NMN lesion causing ipsilateral palatine muscle paralysis), since the uvula moves away from the paralyzed side.
questions.keyConcept: Uvula deviates AWAY from lesioned side (CN X motor).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Reflex cough accompanying ear wash is caused by irritation of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve) innervates the external acoustic meatus; its irritation during ear washing triggers the cough reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Ear wash cough reflex: auricular branch of vagus nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The jugular foramen transmits all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI, and the inferior petrosal sinus; the spinal accessory root (descending from foramen magnum) also passes through but the hypoglossal canal is separate.
questions.keyConcept: Jugular foramen: CN 9,10,11, inferior petrosal sinus (not hypoglossal).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The hypoglossal nerve pierces ……… muscle at the end of its course.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) pierces the genioglossus muscle near its insertion before distributing to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve pierces genioglossus muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Difficulty in protruding the tongue with its deviation to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: Tongue deviation toward the right side during protrusion indicates right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, as the unaffected genioglossus pulls the tongue toward the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviates TOWARD lesioned hypoglossal nerve side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is the chorda tympani nerve (branch of CN VII carrying parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands).
questions.keyConcept: Submandibular ganglion parasympathetic root: chorda tympani (CN VII).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The ……… nerve suspends the pterygopalatine ganglion in its place.
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended by the maxillary nerve (V2) which provides its sensory roots passing through without synapsing.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve suspends pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The largest branch of the vertebral artery is:
questions.explanation: The largest branch of the vertebral artery is the basilar artery, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Largest vertebral branch: basilar artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A branch from the 2nd part of subclavian artery is:
questions.explanation: The second part of subclavian artery gives rise to the internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk (supplying thyroid, neck, and chest wall structures).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery part 2: internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The common carotid artery divides at the level of ……… vertebrae.
questions.explanation: The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4), becoming ICA and ECA.
questions.keyConcept: Common carotid bifurcates at upper border of thyroid cartilage (C4).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The external carotid artery crosses ……… triangles of the neck.
